extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communication, cultural studies, and media theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing communication/media from a cultural perspective that contrasts the 'transmission' and 'ritual' models and situates media in historical, technological, and social context. Intended to guide how to read/interpret newspapers, technologies, and communicative acts as cultural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication defined by terms such as 'imparting,' 'sending,' 'transmitting,' or 'giving information to others'—a metaphor of geography or transportation; the center is the transmission of signals or messages over distance for the purpose of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze media/communication in terms of dissemination, speed, reach, and control. Ask about effects on audiences, whether messages enlighten or obscure, how messages change attitudes or breed credibility/doubt, and the functional/mechanical operations of distribution. Note historical-technological roots (e.g., telegraph, press, canals) and the persistence of metaphors tying communication to transportation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication linked to 'sharing,' 'participation,' 'association,' 'fellowship,' and 'the possession of a common faith'—directed not to extending messages in space but to maintaining society in time and representing shared beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read media acts (e.g., reading a newspaper) as ritual or mass attendance: focus on how presentation confirms a worldview, constructs social roles, dramatizes contending forces, and provides cultural order and satisfaction rather than primarily transmitting new information. Use Durkheimian/anthropological resources to assess how symbolic forms maintain collective life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication as a symbolic process that produces, maintains, repairs, and transforms reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication should be defined and analyzed as a symbolic process whereby reality is produced, maintained, repaired, and transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating communicative acts, attend to the symbolic work they perform (how they construct reality, sustain meanings, mend ruptures, or effect change). Focus analysis on meaning-making practices rather than only on message transmission or behavioral effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze newspapers/media under both transmission and ritual frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasting analytic lenses for newspapers: transmission (instrument for disseminating news and knowledge; mechanical/effects-driven questions) and ritual (a dramatic presentation of the world that confirms roles and a shared worldview).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly contrast the two approaches in media analysis: under transmission ask about content distribution, audience effects, functions/dysfunctions; under ritual examine presentation, dramatization, historical situatedness, invitation to participation, and how news acts as a cultural text or ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical and technological context (transportation, print, telegraph, canals, roads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication and transportation technologies (printing, canals, roads, telegraph, etc.) shape possibilities for political and cultural unity and alter the scale and character of public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess communication phenomena with attention to the material technologies and geographic constraints that enable or limit them. Use historical examples (Jefferson, Madison, Gallatin) to evaluate claims that technologies bind/transform polities and cultures; weigh both hoped-for integrative effects and possible anti-democratic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect origins and metaphors (including religious roots) behind communication concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many concepts of communication (especially the transmission view) have origins in religious metaphors and moral meanings (e.g., movement as redemptive, telegraph as 'What Hath God Wrought').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing claims about communication technologies or functions, interrogate underlying metaphors and their histories. Track moralized or providential language that frames technology as salvific or morally improving, and note how such metaphors persist even after secularization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradictions and ambiguities as analytic resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than trying to resolve tensions (e.g., between transmission and ritual views, or hopes and fears about technology), exploit those contradictions as a source of insight and analytic precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat opposing tendencies (e.g., technology as liberating vs. dominating; communication as binding in space vs. time) as productive tensions to be mined for interpretation. The author recommends leveraging these tensions to 'increase the precision with which we vex one another.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to scale, geography, and political implications of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The size and geography of polities (e.g., continental republic vs. Greek polis) interact with communication modes to produce different civic possibilities and risks (self-sufficiency vs. anonymity; unity vs. faction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communication systems with reference to spatial scale and infrastructural realities: how do transport/communication technologies alter citizens' ability to know one another, distribute representatives, and produce public discourse? Consider both integrative and destabilizing political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat media and technology as cultural actors (machines as expressions of outlooks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology is not merely artifact but actor; machines express and create cultural outlooks and aspirations and reproduce contradictions in miniature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In media analysis, attribute agency in a heuristic sense to technologies: explore how technologies shape practice, imagination, and narratives about progress/restoration. Examine stories told about technologies as part of cultural self-understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an interdisciplinary approach to communication study
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich communication analysis by drawing on sociology, anthropology, history, theology, literature, and related traditions (e.g., Weber, Durkheim, Dewey, Goffman, Geertz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narrow, exhausted behavioral or functional frameworks; incorporate theoretical resources from multiple disciplines to capture symbolic, ritualistic, historical, and social dimensions of communication. Use these resources to 'reopen' analysis and avoid academic stagnation.
